title: Acute Limb Ischaemia: Recognition, Anticoagulation and Vascular Transfer

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected acute limb ischaemia (ALI) in the emergency department (ED) or a hospital without on-site vascular surgery: recognition, Rutherford grading of limb viability, immediate heparin, imaging, reperfusion risks and urgent transfer to a vascular centre. Uses the 2024 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) peripheral artery disease (PAD) guideline (definition and Rutherford table), the UK Defence Medical Services Clinical Guidelines for Operations (CGO) on acute limb ischaemia (2026), the 2025 National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) report, and the US heparin label. Choice of revascularisation technique is for the vascular team and is not covered.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi acute limb ischaemia guideline was found.
The European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) 2020 acute limb ischaemia guideline could not be opened (publisher and archive copies blocked); its recommendations are not used.
Section 11 (Acute Limb Ischemia recommendations) of the ACC/AHA 2024 guideline could not be opened; only the definition (Table 2) and the Rutherford classes (Table 4) are used.
Work-up for the embolic source (electrocardiogram, echocardiography) is not stated in the opened sources and is left to the vascular and medical teams.
Heparin infusion rate and the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) ratio target used locally were not given in the defence guideline; the label target (1.5 to 2 times normal) is shown.
Typical adult normal ranges for potassium, creatinine and creatine kinase are not taken from the guidelines; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute limb ischaemia is a sudden fall in limb perfusion that threatens limb viability (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4). It is called acute when symptoms have lasted 2 weeks or less (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 2; CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management). Causes are embolism, thrombosis in a native artery or in a previous graft or stent, trauma, and peripheral aneurysm with distal embolisation (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4). Nerve and muscle injury follow ischaemia: sensory loss comes first, then weakness, then complete paralysis in an irreversible limb (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4). Restoring flow releases potassium and myoglobin from ischaemic muscle, causing hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia, acute kidney injury (AKI) and acidosis (CGO 2026, Section Think H4AM).

symptoms: Weakness or inability to move the limb (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 2).
Onset within the last 14 days (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).
physicalSigns: Sensory loss: none (class I), toes only (IIa), beyond the toes (IIb), complete (III) (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Motor loss: none (I and IIa), mild to moderate (IIb), complete paralysis (III) (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
redFlags: Sensory loss beyond the toes or any muscle weakness (Rutherford IIb): limb is immediately threatened (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Rutherford IIb: the limb is lost unless revascularised within 6 hours (NCEPOD 2025, Section 1).
Complete sensory and motor loss with no arterial or venous Doppler signal (class III): irreversible (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
After reperfusion: hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia, dark urine (myoglobinuria) or falling urine output (CGO 2026, Section Think H4AM).
precipitants: Thrombosis of a native artery, bypass graft or stent (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Limb trauma, including arterial injury and compartment syndrome (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4; CGO 2026, Section Management of traumatic ALI).
Peripheral aneurysm with distal embolisation (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Symptoms longer than 14 days (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management; ACC/AHA 2024, Table 2).
No sensory or motor loss and audible arterial Doppler signal (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Complete sensory and motor loss with inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Injury mechanism; managed with vascular control, shunt, fasciotomy and fixation sequence (CGO 2026, Section Ortho-vascular Injury).

ruleIn.testName: Hand-held arterial and venous Doppler at the foot
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Arterial signal inaudible (IIa, IIb); arterial and venous both inaudible (III)
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Grades the limb with sensory and motor findings; class IIa and IIb need urgent vascular intervention (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4; CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and grade the limb
actions: Examine sensation, power and foot Doppler signals and assign a Rutherford class (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Record the time of symptom onset (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Give heparin without waiting for imaging
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately once acute limb ischaemia is suspected
actions: Give unfractionated heparin (see Medicines); do not delay it until after imaging (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).
Start supportive treatment with anticoagulation, intravenous fluids and oxygen as soon as possible (NCEPOD 2025, Section 1).

clinicalManagement.title: Call vascular surgery and image
actions: Refer urgently to the vascular team; base the referral on the limb-viability assessment (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).
Get CTA where available (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).
Rutherford IIa and IIb need urgent vascular intervention to restore blood flow (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).

clinicalManagement.title: Transfer threatened limbs to a vascular centre
actions: Transfer Rutherford IIb patients directly to a vascular centre (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.2).
Arrange prompt senior vascular surgery or interventional radiology review (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Watch for reperfusion injury
actions: Monitor potassium, cardiac rhythm, urine colour and output, and creatinine for hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria and AKI (CGO 2026, Section Think H4AM).
Reassess the limb often after surgery and continue analgesia and anticoagulation (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge planning
actions: Give a clear follow-up pathway and risk-reduction measures such as smoking cessation and diabetes referral (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.4).

regimens.indication: Prevent clot propagation in acute limb ischaemia before vascular intervention
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with suspected acute limb ischaemia
regimens.dose: Bolus 75 units/kg intravenously (CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management), then continuous intravenous infusion; the label full-dose regimen is 5000 units intravenously, then 20,000 to 40,000 units per 24 hours in 1000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride, adjusted to the aPTT (Heparin label, Section 2.4).
regimens.route: Intravenous bolus then continuous intravenous infusion
regimens.duration: Until definitive vascular treatment and the vascular team's anticoagulation plan
adjustments: Target aPTT 1.5 to 2 times normal (Heparin label, Section 2.3).
No renal or hepatic dose change in the label; use caution in liver disease with impaired haemostasis (Heparin label, Section 5.2).
Chronic renal failure raises the risk of hyperkalaemia; check potassium (Heparin label, Section 5.9).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: aPTT, international normalised ratio (INR) and platelet count at baseline; aPTT about every 4 hours during infusion (Heparin label, Section 2.3; CGO 2026, Section Initial Assessment & Management).
Potassium in patients at risk (Heparin label, Section 5.9).
contraindications: History of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, with or without thrombosis (Heparin label, Section 4).
Known hypersensitivity to heparin or pork products (Heparin label, Section 4).
Coagulation tests cannot be done at suitable intervals (Heparin label, Section 4).
Uncontrolled active bleeding, except from disseminated intravascular coagulation (Heparin label, Section 4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Limb hypoperfusion of 2 weeks or less with pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paraesthesia and/or paralysis (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 2).
No sensory loss, no motor loss, arterial and venous Doppler audible (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Sensory loss of toes only, no motor loss, arterial Doppler inaudible, venous Doppler audible (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Sensory loss beyond the toes, mild to moderate weakness, arterial Doppler inaudible, venous Doppler audible (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).
Complete sensory loss, paralysis, arterial and venous Doppler inaudible (ACC/AHA 2024, Table 4).

teaching.scope: Adults with suspected acute limb ischaemia (ALI) in the emergency department (ED) or a hospital without on-site vascular surgery: recognition, Rutherford grading of limb viability, immediate heparin, imaging, reperfusion risks and urgent transfer to a vascular centre. Uses the 2024 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) peripheral artery disease (PAD) guideline (definition and Rutherford table), the UK Defence Medical Services Clinical Guidelines for Operations (CGO) on acute limb ischaemia (2026), the 2025 National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) report, and the US heparin label. Choice of revascularisation technique is for the vascular team and is not covered.
learningObjectives: Grade a threatened limb with the Rutherford classes.
Know the 6-hour window for Rutherford IIb.
pitfalls: Treating IIb as non-urgent because the foot is warm proximally.
keyPoints: Sensory loss beyond the toes or any weakness means IIb: transfer now.
Heparin should not wait for CTA.
A silent venous Doppler signal suggests an irreversible limb.

patientEducation: A blocked artery in the leg or arm needs treatment within hours to save the limb.
After treatment, report new pain, numbness, swelling or dark urine at once.
Take blood thinners exactly as prescribed after discharge.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; vascular surgeon; interventional radiologist; anaesthetist; intensive care unit (ICU) for reperfusion injury; diabetes and smoking-cessation services (NCEPOD 2025, Sections 4.2 and 4.4).
dischargeCriteria: Limb perfused and stable after revascularisation; potassium and creatinine stable; anticoagulation plan agreed by the vascular team; follow-up pathway and risk-reduction referrals arranged (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.4).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Vascular clinic follow-up as set by the treating team; smoking-cessation and diabetes referral (NCEPOD 2025, Section 4.4).
